# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven 'for' cells on a 0 to 7 axis with the marker at 6 labelled 'at least 8 in 10', so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The actor, the 7-day window and 'lose the thread' are my words, but prevalence was not one of the two beliefs I checked on the way in, so it reads as Keel's framing of my idea rather than a line I signed off.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7' plus a pointer to the next two cards tells me to read on, but not what this means for AirCaps, such as 'the problem is everyday, so lead with it and test how much it costs them'.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible ('7 answered · 7 counted'), the small group is named as 'a lean, not a call', and the So line limits the claim to 'these 7'.
screens.instead: Holding up, 7 of 7 lost the thread this week against a bar of 6 of 7. Only 7 people, so it is a lean, but the problem shows up weekly; whether it is frequent and painful enough to pay $599 for is the next two cards.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' sits right beside the count that decides it: 4 of 7 at or beyond my 4 to 7 days against a bar of 5 of 7, so 1 short.
screens.why_b2: The axis plainly counts days out of 7 with the median at 4, but the bar is drawn as '5 of 7' people on a days axis, and the legend ('what you said / at what you said / short of it') takes a second look to see which cells are mine.
screens.why_b3: Frequency, 4 to 7 days out of 7, losing the thread with hearing people: that is the band and the wording I set on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' defers rather than telling me what to do, such as whether to widen the band to 2 to 7 days or narrow my segment to people who are in group settings daily.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, it says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and a 4-to-3 split is called a disagreement rather than a near-hold; the stray 'the most recent time it happened' under a days-count question is odd but claims nothing.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 lose the thread on 4 or more days and 3 on fewer, 1 short of your bar on 7 people. Most people have this problem but not daily, so either set your band at 2 to 7 days or test whether the 3 low-frequency people are the quieter-week hearing-aid users you would not target first.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '7 of 7 put it in their two · bar 5 of 7', so I know it held and by how much it cleared my bar.
screens.why_b2: The caption makes clear the bars count 14 picks from 7 people and the bar is at 5 of 7, but the strip under it reads 'for 7, against 7' on a 7-person strip, and the other options are each tagged 'against', so I need a second look to see that nobody was actually against me.
screens.why_b3: The title 'Importance' and the belief line are word for word what I checked, and 'Losing the thread of fast conversation' is my wording.
screens.why_b4: The So line usefully warns that this means top two, not first, but it doesn't tell me what to do next, for example that fast group conversation is a safe lead for the wedge and that 'getting a word in' (3 picks) is the runner-up worth watching for the two-way gap.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' is said plainly, but the strip's 'against 7' and the 'against' tags on the other options read as if people counted against me when all 7 counted for me.
screens.instead: Show the strip as 7 cells, 7 for and 0 against, label the other options 'also picked' rather than 'against', and end with: 'With 7 of 7 it's a safe lead for the pitch; getting a word in (3) is the second pain to watch.'

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: Each answer is labelled for or against with its count, the line marks where 'fell short' starts, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against, with the marker at 5. Everything reads on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Current solution and the belief is the line I checked word for word: hearing aids or phone captions still falling short.
screens.why_b4: "Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study" points forward, but it doesn't tell me what the gap means for the glasses, for instance that half of these people get the gist but lose the details, so captions have to carry the specifics.
screens.why_b5: It sticks to 'these 7', says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and shows the 3 who were in the worst outcomes without inflating them.
screens.instead: Today's way falls short for 6 of these 7: half get the gist but lose the details, half lose the thread and nod along. The glasses have to give back the details, not just the gist, and that is the bar the next study holds them to.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on 'Holding up' with '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7' right beside it, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b3: The line is named 'Current solution' and my belief about hearing aids and phone captions falling short is printed word for word.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this means for AirCaps. The screen is headed 'When a line fails', yet the line that actually split, Frequency, is waved off with 'a number has no why worth a question', so I get no steer on the one result that disagreed.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and the hold is not inflated, but 'When a line fails' sits over a line that held, and nothing flags that 7 people is a thin base for 'most'.
screens.why_b6: Tomás's 'deaf on one side, I take the end seat' shows that single-sided hearing loss has a free seating workaround, which suggests unilateral users are a weaker wedge than my segment line implied.
screens.instead: Current solution held 6 of 7 (small n). The one holdout is deaf on one side and manages by seating, so lead with bilateral and severe loss. Frequency split 4/3, so check how many days a week the hard conversations really happen.

screens.why1: As the first question it makes sense: it checks I'm someone who deals with hearing people regularly before asking anything else.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is my own everyday word, but "talk" makes me pause, because I'm not sure whether texting, emailing or chatting through an interpreter counts, or only face to face.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether I've been with hearing people this week: at work, at the shop, at the doctor's.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it for a screener, and no escape is needed here.
screens.why5: It asks exactly who the study is for, and nothing about a product or a company's plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It's short and one question, and "I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No." is a little stiff but easy to hold; "Yes or no" would sound more natural.
screens.instead: Do you talk face to face with hearing people every week? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether one of those conversations got away from me this week, though the kicker still says 1 of 4 as if I hadn't moved on.
screens.why2: Losing the thread is exactly how I'd describe it: nodding along and then realising I've no idea what they're on about now.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether that happened to me this week; it happens most weeks at work or at dinner.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but a gate shouldn't carry escapes at all, and these two are odd: one is a whole sentence about recalling one particular conversation, which doesn't answer a yes-or-no about the week, and the other is an 'I'd rather not say' that shouldn't exist.
screens.why5: Nothing of anyone's product leaks to me, but the question drops the face-to-face part and the too fast or too noisy cause, so a video call or a phone call I lost track of would count as a yes too.
screens.why6: Heard once with 'Yes or no.' it is short, one question and easy to answer.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, was a face-to-face conversation with hearing people too fast or too noisy for you to follow? Yes · No (no escape chips)

screens.why1: I just said yes, I lost the thread this week, so asking how many days that happened is the natural next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: Losing the thread is exactly how I'd put it, and counting days in the last week is clear on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know which days I was at work meetings, the shop counter or family dinner and couldn't keep up, so I can count them honestly.
screens.why4: One to seven covers every possible answer after my yes, the numbers can't overlap, and I can't recall fits if the week has blurred together.
screens.why5: It asks only about my own conversations with hearing people, and nothing about a product or anyone's plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question, the range from 1 to 7 is easy to hold, and the escape is said last and briefly.

screens.why1: After asking how often I lost the thread, it makes sense to ask which part of talking with hearing people I would most like to be easier.
screens.why2: Most of it is plain, but 'made easier' paired with 'Losing the thread of fast conversation' reads backwards, since I want that to stop, not get easier, so I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: Every one of these is something I deal with in an ordinary week, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: The last option is phrased the wrong way round, and the one I would most likely pick, following talk in a noisy restaurant or a group, is not there, while phone calls and announcements are not face-to-face talk at all.
screens.why5: The founder's situation is face-to-face talk that is too fast or too noisy, but noise has dropped out and phone calls and station announcements have crept in.
screens.why6: Five short options I can hold when I hear them once, but 'losing the thread of fast conversation' sounds wrong after 'made easier' and makes me stop and think.
screens.instead: Think of your last week of talking with hearing people. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Keeping up when people talk fast; following talk in noisy places; following a group talking at once; getting a word in at the right moment; or not being worn out by listening. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: After I picked what I'd most like made easier, asking how my last conversation actually went with what I use now is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: The stem says my last conversation but then asks how following conversations went, plural, and it lumps hearing aids and phone captions together, so I had to read it twice to know which one it meant.
screens.why3: Partly: plenty of us lipread, use an interpreter or just ask people to repeat, and some don't use hearing aids or captions at all, so I'd have to guess or fudge it.
screens.why4: The five steps from followed nearly everything to could not follow it at all are distinct and sound like how I'd describe it, and I can't recall fits as the way out.
screens.why5: Naming hearing aids or phone captions pushes a particular kind of tool at me, and the switch from one conversation to conversations in general reads like a template pasted over the founder's simpler question.
screens.why6: The options say well, but hearing aids or phone captions, followed by the shift from my last conversation to conversations in general, is a mouthful to take in by ear in one go.
screens.instead: Think of your last face-to-face conversation with hearing people. How much of it did you follow? Followed nearly everything said; missed a little, caught up quickly; caught the gist, missed the details; lost the thread and mostly nodded along; could not follow it at all; or I can't recall.
